To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

dietary K+ loading and deficiency have distinct effects on renal sodium transporters and blood pressure in mice, but do not recapitulate inverse effects of potassium intake on blood pressure seen in humans.
the commonly used extreme dietary potassium maneuvers in mice do not recapitulate inverse effects of dietary potassium on blood pressure in humans.

dietary potassium deficiency and excess did not recapitulated the inverse effects of dietary potassium on blood pressure in humans, and this may be due to extreme potassium stress, low Na+:K+, duration of treatment, development of diabetes insipidis and other coinciding events.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effects of dietary potassium on blood pressure and sodium transport, and the results have implications for the development of hypertension in the setting of dietary potassium deficiency or excess.
the role that dietary potassium plays in regulating blood pressure.
the effects of dietary potassium stress on blood volume, blood pressure, and sodium and potassium handling in the kidney.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dietary potassium manipulations used here did not reproduce the inverse relationship between blood pressure and potassium observed in epidemiologic studies.
the effects of potassium stress are complex and not easily recapitulated in a short term animal study.

potassium deficiency is associated with diabetes insipidu, while potassium excess is associated with increased blood pressure, but the mechanisms by which these occur are complex and not yet fully understood.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effects of potassium on the renal handling of sodium and on blood pressure depend on the dietary potassium concentration, the Na:K+ ratio, and other factors.
dietary potassium loading and potassium depletion do not affect blood pressure in a similar manner as seen in epidemiological studies.
the dietary maneuvers we used here did not reproduce the inverse effects of dietary potassium on blood pressure in mice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of dietary K+ on blood pressure are likely to be more complex than previously assumed and that dietary K+ should be considered as an important variable in the study of hypertension.

dietary potassium loading is a powerful tool to study the regulation of renal ion transport and blood pressure, and that the effects of high dietary potassium on blood pressure are likely mediated by changes in the renal handling of Na+.
dietary potassium stress is a powerful regulator of blood pressure and renal ion transport and can have a dramatic effect on the development of salt-sensitive hypertension.
